subsubtopic: BRUNDTLAND REPORT-SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT CONCEPT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Throne Speech the Government proclaims its support for sustainable development, but a commitment to implementing it at home and abroad is simply not there.
There is no commitment to implement sustainable development by way of reviewing budgets, programs and policies in key Departments such as energy, agriculture, fisheries, finance, forestry, regional development, transport, defence, northern development, international aid, science and technology. In addition, we learn the federal Government will only participate in the establishment of a Centre on Sustainable Development in Winnipeg, a retreat from the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) commitment last year to the UN General Assembly. There is not a word about climate warming, about energy policies, about integrating the economy with the environment.
We are afraid that the Government is preaching rather than practising, and prefers image over substance. Canadians believe that to pay lip service to the Brundtland Report is not good enough.

subsubtopic: DEATHS OF CAMROSE FAMILY IN PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today in Camrose, Alberta, a small Prairie city of 16,000 persons, a memorial service will be held to bereave the untimely death of a young family of fine people.
Tony Deis, 35; his wife Marilyn, 34, and their three daughters, Amanda, 10, Jaclyn, 7, and Kimberly, 5, were all killed in a plane crash near Newport, California.
My home city is in shock. Local citizens are still trying to comprehend the magnitude of this unfortunate tragedy. This was a family with unusual talent who worked extensively for the betterment of their community. Everyone who met them thought of them as friends.
On this hollow and unhappy day, the citizens of Camrose grieve. May we, as a collective House of parliamentarians, take some time on this day to reflect on the sadness of this occasion and be reminded of the fragility of life.
Camrose and Canada have lost a family of extraordinary fine character. May we all share in the sorrow.

subtopic: DUBIN INQUIRY-ACTION TAKEN BY ONTARIO TRACK AND FIELD ASSOCIATION
DUBIN INQUIRY-ACTION TAKEN BY ONTARIO TRACK AND FIELD ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that nothing be done to impede the Dubin Inquiry's pursuit of the truth about the use of banned substances in Canadian and international sport.
The Ontario Track and Field Association's action in withdrawing the records of athletes who have told the truth to the Dubin Inquiry is a blatant threat to the due process of the inquiry which was established with the support of all Parties in the House.

To do otherwise will be treated by the Government and this House as intentional interference in the inquiry and a contempt of Parliament under whose legislation the inquiry was established.
I ask the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest) to step into this matter today. It is time the Minister got tough with sports groups that prejudge the inquiry and interfere with its work. We in this House will

subsubtopic: NAMIBIA-PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN PERSONNEL IN OBSERVER FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Nations is in the process of sending to Namibia a UN observer force which includes 247 Canadians to supervise the withdrawal of South African troops and SWAPO from Namibia. Since last weekend, approximately 190 rebel troops and Namibian police have been killed in battle. This represents the heaviest fighting and the largest military incursion by guerrilla forces in the 23-year war between South Africa and SWAPO.
The South Africa Government has now demanded that the UN force, presently numbering 1,000 and including 65 Canadian personnel, take immediate action to prevent further SWAPO incursions and to enforce the peace agreement or it will abrogate the treaty and initiate its own military action. The security and safety of Canadian troops appears to be threatened by this dangerous escalation of the conflict.
I call on the Government to inform the House of the status of our peacekeeping force and to make clear what contingency plans it has to ensure the safety of our troops and to secure peace in Namibia.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF INGLIS CLOTHES WASHING MACHINE PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the men and women who make half of Canada's clothes washing machines intend to go on making them for Canadians. Soon after the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal came into force, the Inglis Corporation, 70 per cent owned by Whirlpool in the U.S.A., announced that it will close its only washing machine factory located on Stra-chan Avenue in Trinity-Spadina. It plans to supply the Canadian market from its huge, newly equipped plant in Ohio.
April 5, 1989

Within days, 600 enthusiastic plant workers, members of Local 2900, United Steelworkers of America, declared they would mobilize to take over the plant and continue making washing machines for Canadians. Their union, which has carried through half a dozen successful worker buyouts in the United States, bringing moneylosing plants back to economic health, is convinced it can do that with the profitable Strachan Avenue enterprise.
Toronto's Mayor Eggleton has agreed to ask Toronto City Council to contribute to the cost of the feasibility study and protect the manufacturing zoning of the Strachan Avenue site. Canada's capitalists may be quitting but Canadian workers will take over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PLAQUE COMMEMORATING INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1942 Japanese Canadians were uprooted from their homes, relocated, and interned in camps or deported, because of unrealistic fears and discrimination. On April 1, 40 years to the day that the Government of Canada restored full rights to Japanese Canadians, I attended a plaque unveiling ceremony commemorating their internment at the very site of the staging facility used in the 40s, the Pacific National Exhibition grounds in Vancouver.
The plaque, in English, French, and Japanese, follows up the Prime Minister's announcement last September of a redress settlement for Japanese Canadians. I would like to give special recognition to 88-year-old Reverend Canon Gordon Nakayama of the Diocese of New Westminster who, in a clear, strong voice, described what it was like in 1942 when he had to help comfort the Japanese Canadians who were being forcibly relocated. He then stated: "Now I think Canada is the best country in the world."

subsubtopic: CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few weeks, Canadian consumers have been
subjected to skyrocketing credit card interest rates. This is not the first time in the Government's history that consumers have suffered as a result of rising credit card interest rates. If the Government maintains its hands-off policy on this issue, it certainly will not be the last.
In March of 1987 recommendations proposed by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, together with the threat by the then Minister of State for Finance, the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Hockin), managed temporarily to lower the interest charge on unpaid credit card balances. Canadian consumers need a commitment from the Government that they will be adequately protected from the recurrence of rising interest rates in 1989. The Government must ensure that consumers are not victimized by these excessive fees.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN DAIRY INDUSTRY-RETENTION OF MARKETING BOARDS URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to represent the federal riding of Oxford which many colleagues will know is the daily capital of Canada. Both the dairy industiy and Canadians have benefited from a supply management system run by efficient provincial milk marketing boards. As a result, Canadians enjoy dairy products of the highest quality and at price increases well below the cost of living.
I would like to urge our Government and our GATT negotiating officials to resist very strenuously any movement to eliminate or compromise on Article XI of the agreement. In its present form and interpretation, Article XI does not consider domestic marketing boards as providing unfair advantage in international trade.
Further, Canada's milk supply management program which is the envy of many other countries contains the elements for ensuring that world markets are not oversupplied with low-priced dairy products. Thus, the focus of our participation at the GATT negotiations should be on agricultural export subsidies and not on Article XI and our own domestic supply system.

speechtext:

Yesterday the Canadian Aviation Safety Board released two recommendations in response to the three near misses in December, 1988, and in January of this year. It called upon the Minister to implement new safety measures to protect the Canadian traveler. The Minister need not wait the required 90 days since the report says, and I quote.
"These problems should be addressed without delay".

Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra:) My first reaction to the Throne Speech is that the document is not a confident agenda of a Government heading into its second mandate. Indeed, it is a tired repetition of some of the same old lines we have heard before. It is not as if the Government has not had enough time. It has had 97 days to explain to Canadians whether it intends to break election promises, raise taxes or cut expenditures. After waiting all this time, we now know that the Government intends to do all three. Canadians are going to get
shafted by the Mulroney Government, shafted by a new regressive and inflationary value added tax or consumption tax; shafted by tax increases; shafted by a policy of high interest rates; shafted by the Prime Minister's broken promises on investment programs and shafted by changes to the unemployment insurance system.
What about child care? We have just a vague promise. There is no commitment to legislation. There is no commitment to do anything about post-secondary education in this country when most Canadians recognize that education is the key to our future. There is not a word in this speech about the housing crisis. There is no mention of minority language rights. Air safety is not mentioned. There is no mention of the renewal of the ERDA agreements, fundamental as they are to regional equality and regional development in the country. What about the commitment in the speech to do something about predatory overfishing on the Atlantic coast three days after this Government sold out Newfoundland to the French? What about the claim in the speech that the Government's regional development programs are working well? Tell that to Atlantic Canadians. Tell that to people in northern and eastern Ontario. Tell that to people in western Canada. How about yet another promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to clean up the ethics of his own Government? That will hold until the next scandal.
Speaking of scandals, Mr. Speaker. I was pleased about one feature of the Throne Speech. I was pleased that the Governor General was permitted to read the speech herself. After his recent breakthrough at the Academy Awards, I was surprised that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) did not try to elbow Her Excellency out of the way!

speechtext:
There are presidential tendencies by this Government and this Prime Minister but at least that decorum was maintained.
As is the tradition, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Speech from the Throne, the Hon. Members for Calgary Southeast (Mr. Richardson) and Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau) respectively. Considering the limited material that they had to work with, I felt that they were fertile in terms of creativity, did the best that they could, and indeed made excellent personal speeches.
April 5, 1989

We are happy to welcome our new members, men and women from all regions in this country, including the Territories. They are taking their first steps in Parliament, but they are dedicated, hardworking, observant and very determined to represent their constituents effectively.
Mr. Speaker, you may rely on our full co-operation in maintaining the high standards, dignity and discipline expected in this House. However, I wish to inform the Prime Minister it is our firm resolve to form a vigilant and vigourous opposition. We intend to remind the Government as often as necessary that Canada is not the private domain of the rich and powerful, of the businessmen of this country. This country also belongs to people across Canada who cannot make ends meet. There are businessmen who try to make a profit at any cost, but there are people across this country who are suffering and who need the assistance of governments at both levels.

Parliament, except for two weeks in December, has not been sitting for six months. As Parliamentarians we have had a wasted winter. After the November election we were called back only briefly to accede to the trade deal. We lived up to our commitments. Since then the Government has been on autopilot, drifting, delaying the recall of the House. Meanwhile, Canadians have been caught, hit with sky-rocketing interest rates, accelerated concentration of economic power in the hands of fewer and fewer people; foreign take-overs, mergers. American Express has come to Canada and it is "not going home without it". In fact, we have given them a bag.
Air safety is in chaos. Talking about air transport, there has been nothing but ministerial sloppiness and incompetence. Following the Gander crash we demanded a full public inquiry. The Government denied that there was a problem, yet the Canadian Aviation Safety Board gave the Government a split decision on the reasons for the crash. We needed a public inquiry. Safety warnings were not passed on to the airlines in time. Twenty-four people lost their lives in the Dryden crash. An assistant Deputy Minister of Transport was fired. There was confusion and turmoil in the Department. Canadians are worried. Are our skies safe? We have two Ministers and
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
neither one is doing the job. There is ministerial incompetence, and departmental chaos.
Where is the plan to deal with spiralling interest rates? Where is the plan to deal with the devastating impact that those rates are having across the country? How high will the Government allow these rates to go? How high will the Minister accede to the Governor's wish to push them higher and higher, 14, 15, or 16 per cent. Where does it stop? I suppose we must await the Budget.
After spending four years of slashing the budgets of environmental programs, of ravaging Environment Canada, the Government and the Prime Minister had a deathbed repentance during the election and they discovered finally what the Throne Speech eloquently calls the environmental imperative. It talks of limits on toxic chemicals, improving water quality, protecting the Arctic, and an acid rain treaty with the United States. We understand that vocabulary here; that was our program.
There is also something called an environmental partners' fund to encourage awareness of the environment. We do not need anything as Canadians to make us more aware of the environment. Canadians are aware of the environment. They know that four years of inaction and budget cuts have taken a severe toll on the efforts of Canadians to meet the environmental challenge ahead of us. Canadians want action and not rhetoric. So far all we have seen is the Prime Minister grandstanding at an environmental conference in Europe.
The following is what the respected international environmental group Friends of the Earth had to say about Canada and two of the other countries at that conference in The Hague. "Particularly hypocritical are the Canadian, Dutch, and Italian Governments which have in turn slashed energy efficiency and conservation budgets in recent years." So much for that award. The Prime Minister in this type of posture is embarrassing all of us. I challenge him to get serious.
If last night's debate is any indication of the preparedness of this Government on environmental matters when we debated on an emergency status the Alaska Canada oil spill, then the Government is hopelessly unprepared. The policy announced last night was "Don't worry Canadians, it will all blow away." Wait for the right tides, wait for the right winds, and pray to God that nothing happens. That was the policy of the Minister of the Environment(Mr. Bouchard).

April 5, 1989
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Shame!

Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister shouted from the roof tops that Canadian men and women should vote for his party because, and I quote: "We can manage this country. We can manage change." But where did all those change managers go? They vanished into thin air. The only memorable incident since then was a statement by the Minister of Finance who solemnly informed us that his Government did not intend to keep its election promises. No less! The only statement in four months!
During the campaign, the same Minister of Finance made a very clear distinction between the Government's policies and election promises. He denigrated our platform. Our political platform was just a bunch of election promises but the Government's election promises were commitments! Quite a difference! He defended that position seriously, talking about billions of dollars that would be spent. Well, we were wrong to believe the Minister of Finance.
Before the House resumed sitting, the Minister had already changed his mind. He put all those billions back in his pocket, because today, four months later, we can no longer afford to spend them. Mr. Speaker, this Government, this Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance have fooled us with their promises. This Government has quite simply deceived Canadians across the country.
It is quite obvious they never had the slightest intention of keeping their word or meeting their commitments. They were only interested in buying Canadian voters, in buying the election so they could sell this country at a discount to the Americans.

During the last election the Liberal Party fought what we believe was a good, tough, and clean campaign. We talked about the issues. We talked about losing control over the economic and social levers necessary to shape our future, and the disastrous impact the trade deal will have on this country because it abandons those levers and surrenders our sovereignty.
We were told by the Prime Minister, when he launched the negotiations with the United States, that the sole purpose of a primary bilateral deal with the U.S. was secure access into the American market. We told him that that meant two things. It meant an exception from American protectionist trade law, and it also meant a dispute settlement mechanism to enforce that exemption. The issue of secure access to the American market was never discussed or defended by the Prime Minister during the last election, and with reason.
Under Articles 1902 and 1904 of the trade agreement, American trade law, countervail, antidumping, surtax, and quotas can still be applied against Canadian exports. Under the American Statutes of 1930, the Trade Act of 1974, and the Omnibus Trade Bill of 1988, the same laws still apply against our lumber, our potash, our steel, our fish, and they are still to be applied on a daily basis by the Americans. True, we have a dispute mechanism. We have a tribunal headed-up on our side, coincidentally, by strong supporters of the deal. This tribunal cannot challenge American law. Under the agreement, it can only apply that law against American judicial precedent and practice.
Those on our side who were fortunate enough to meet with the senior members of the U.S. Congress and who asked if there was any way to negotiate a more secure access to the U.S. market were told by Senators on the Republic democratic side that there is no way the United States Congress would ever yield its jurisdiction over trade law. That being so, the sole purpose of this deal was not obtained. It is not a free trade agreement. It is not even a trade deal. It is the Sale of Canada Act.
Look what we gave away! Energy. Americans wanted secure access to our energy, and they got it, especially in times of shortage. The same regime applies to all our renewable and non-renewable resources, including water.
There is now an explosion of plans to export trillions of cubic metres of natural gas from our Arctic. I welcome that development for the people of the Territories. However, since deregulation, gas exports to the United States have increased by over 70 per cent. This is going to continue. Because of the proportionality regime in the trade deal, we could find ourselves as Canadians locked into supplying 60 to 65 per cent of our gas to the United States at bargain basement prices. Once those volumes are established, we are bound by those volumes under
April 5, 1989

the trade agreement. The upcoming National Energy Board hearings do not make much difference because that body has been turned into nothing more than a monitoring agency with no authority to limit or change export levels.
Agriculture. We on this side of the House told the Government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ma-zankowski) that there was no way we could contemplate free trade in agriculture. Our climates are too different. Our growing season is shorter. Our costs are higher. Our burdens are heavier. Yet our farmers' cash crops, vegetables, fruits, and horticulture and everything that was protected by marketing boards is now thrown into direct competition with the farmers of California, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi and Alabama. They have a 12-month growing season, and our farmers are caught in a climate they have been dealing with for over two centuries in a very courageous fashion.
The agricultural supply-management system will be negotiated away. We were warned that food processing would move out. Quaker Oats, Heinz and McCain's have already said they are leaving.
Fishing. We have talked about fishing in this House, but what this agreement did was give up our rights under GATT There is no exemption in favour of our fishing people or our fishing processors as the Government claims.
Control over foreign investment. The screening has evaporated to a limit of $150 million on a direct acquisition and no limit on an indirect takeover. We now have unlimited takeovers. In anticipation of the trade deal, the increase in foreign ownership was under way prior to the election. According to Investment Canada's report for 1987-88, foreign takeovers, 70 per cent of which were American, increased sharply to $22.2 billion worth of investment, up from $12.5 billion the year before. American business is now poised under the deal to pick up Canadian companies at bargain basement prices.
Capital markets. We said repeatedly that our banking insurance and investment industries are now wide open to American penetration, particularly banking. We do not have any reciprocal rights into the American market, primarily because of state jurisdiction over banking and the prohibition against linking banking and investment under the American legislation. We do not have reciprocal rights. American Express was at our doors the very day of the election, and they will be the first of many.
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
During the election campaign, we won the battle for the minds and hearts of Canadians. On the trade issue, more than one and a half million people voted against that deal than voted for it.

We won the message. The message was winning the election for us. The Conservatives did not respond to our message on trade, a message that Canadians were concerned about. They attacked the messenger. They launched an unprecedented, personal attack on my character, sincerity and competence. Their negative ad campaign was a textbook model to be studied for obvious comparisons to similar events south of the border.
We also saw the unprecedented intervention of big business with millions of dollars, uncovered by the Election Expenses Act, in an advertising campaign in support of the deal.
We saw democracy stripped of its majesty. It was a cynical manipulation of public opinion, a power-hungry reach for the lower side of human nature. The Government was playing to fear and not to the pride of a nation.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say again to the Prime Minister: You have a tarnished mandate. You have a sullied victory. You bought an election and sold out a country, and Canadians will not allow this country to be sold out!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Over four million Canadians have supported the Liberal Party. Fifty-seven per cent of Canadians voted against the deal. Canadians in eight out of ten provinces voted against the deal. We will continue to oppose the trade deal in accordance with the mandate given to us by those who supported us. We will seek to lessen its negative impact on Canadians by promoting adequate adjustment programs, programs the Prime Minister guaranteed Canadians would be in place in time to prevent any hardships that might follow the deal. Once again, the Prime Minister has made promises that he will not and cannot keep.
How often did we hear from the Prime Minister that the trade deal was not going to hurt anybody? The Prime Minister and his friends in the business community knew that thousands of workers ran the risk of losing their jobs in the so-called "rationalization" of North American business. The Prime Minister said it would not be a problem because his Government would bring in adjustment programs. We all remember that.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
Now we have the long-awaited de Grandpre Commission appointed by this Government. Mr. de Grandpre and his colleagues have stated that there cannot be adjustment programs targeted to help those who are hurt by the trade deal. The reason he says there can be no specific programs to ease the pain is that the impact of the trade deal is so large and varied. Once more, either the Prime Minister did not know what he was talking about, did not know the facts, or simply did not want to let the facts interfere with his story during the election campaign.
It is now the duty of this Prime Minister and Government to provide Canadian workers with adequate adjustment programs. On this side of the House we will insist that they be sensible programs directed specifically to the workers who will pay for the Prime Minister's trade deal with their jobs, financial insecurity and social dislocation.
We also intend to be vigilant and watchful during the five to seven years of negotiation on the definition of "subsidy". Those subsidy negotiations are critical for us. They will define what future Canadian Governments can or cannot do for individuals and for the disadvantaged regions of the country. Canada has agreed under the deal to negotiate for the next five to seven years over what is an allowable subsidy. The real negotiations are now under way. This Government signed a trade deal with the United States before all its terms were negotiated or signed. That is like signing a real estate contract to sell your house before you have agreed to negotiate the terms. The Americans have aggressively stated, their goals in these negotiations. They include removal of the exemption for Canadian culture, an end to any investment screening of business, a definition of an unfair subsidy as any Canadian Government, law, regulation, or practice that is "an adverse impact upon American business and producers".
This is a vital issue facing Canada. This vital issue facing us in the next few years is the negotiation of subsidy. Yet there is not a single word about these negotiations in the text of the Throne Speech.

Who is going to negotiate for us? Will the provinces be involved? Will we, as Members of the House of Commons who, after all, represent Canadians, be informed of all the aspects of these negotiations? The Prime Minister made a solemn commitment that social programs and regional development would never be affected, but we have heard all this before. We have heard this tune many times. We have also heard the Prime Minister refer to our social programs as a sacred trust, but that did not keep him from trying to deindex old age pensions. Today, the threat looms even larger, when we hear the Prime Minister's friends, Canadian businessmen, demanding cutbacks in our social programs. Incredible, what a difference a few months make in the Conservative vocabulary! During the last election campaign, social programs had once again become inviolate and sacred. In Quebec City, taking his own mother as witness, the Prime Minister said, and I quote:
Why would I want to hurt my mother?
In public, businessmen claimed that the Mulroney agreement had nothing to do with social programs and would have no impact on them.
However, even before the election we thought there was something fishy when we read the September bulletin of the Conseil du patronat. In its bulletin, the Conseil du patronat maintains that to remain competitive with the United States and with their American rivals, Quebec businessmen should no longer be required to finance certain health insurance programs.
More recently, the President of the Manufacturers Association, Mr. Laurent Thibault, wanted the Government to reduce the deficit by cutting certain social programs because, and I quote:
They undermine our ability to make the transition to free trade.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce sings the same tune. Pressure on our social programs does not have to come from the United States. The Prime Minister's friends are quite capable of bringing that pressure to bear themselves.

The trade issue will haunt this Parliament and our country. It has added fuel to the merger mania. It has thrown open our businesses to American takeovers. I have heard the arguments-synergism, more efficiency, more productivity-but in a world where the Japanese have led the way into the smaller decision-making groups, to bringing decisions to the work floor and the factory, I have never seen convincing proof.
April 5, 1989

Where are the new jobs as a result of these mergers and takeovers? Where is the new technology? Where are the new ideas? Where is the new efficiency? The case has not been proven. I say once again that the trade deal is takeovers unlimited. It is what the economists call the rationalization of North American businesses, rationalization in favour of American businesses at the expense of Canadian workers.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, you read about it every day. No sooner was the election over than there were plant closings, mergers, takeovers, Gillette, British Footwear, Northern Telecom, Texaco, Wardair, Consolidated Bathurst. The list goes on and on.
Combine that growing concentration of economic power in Montreal, in Toronto, especially across the border, with the deregulation and privatization of our transport services in this country sponsored by this Government-Air Canada, VIA Rail, Canadian National-and you have the trend toward the shutting down of rural and small town Canada.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity in private legal practice to appear in several major cases before the regulatory agencies of this country and of the provinces. There used to be a phrase in our statutes: "Public convenience and necessity". It meant that anyone who wanted a licence to transport goods or people across this country had to prove public necessity, had to prove public convenience and had to prove that equal service would be given to Canadians no matter where they lived in this country. That has been eliminated and now market forces are king.
Privatization. We have seen before our eyes the elimination and dissipation and dilution of the public infrastructure of transportation in this country, publicly owned, again to ensure that there was equal service no matter where you live. Now the service of Air Canada has been cut-Stephenville, Sydney-I could go through all the communities. The same fares will be paid, but not the same service, not the same style of aircraft. We are getting to a situation with VIA Rail. What have the Conservatives argued for years in opposition? They argued that VIA Rail should be strengthened, that we should have high speed passenger trains, particularly on the Quebec City/Windsor corridor, that we should have high speed trains to allow us to compete with other industrial nations to take the load off the airports, off
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
our highways which are becoming more and more congested around our major cities and to reduce automobile pollution.
In 1985 the Deputy Prime Minister said this: It is now time to turn VIA into a strong system that is cost effective, national in scope and one which Canadians will be proud of and will use. That is the Member of Parliament from Vegreville.
The current Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) is now contemplating the elimination of passenger rail service in this country supported by the Prime Minister who says use it or lose it, quoting statistics that only 20 per cent of it is being used anyway.
Well, he is wrong again. The proper figure according to VIA is 52.4 per cent with even higher capacity on lines in more populous areas. As my colleague from Miramichi has put it so well, if the Prime Minister is determined to scuttle VIA Rail, the least we can expect is he tell the public the truth.

speechtext: That would be a switch.

We now know that the Liberal Members are being joined by the Atlantic Members who are expressing the same concerns, that if this is a free parliamentary system, we want to see those Atlantic Members from the Conservative Party join us in protesting what has happened.

I notice that the Hon. Member for Annapolis is keeping his counsel and his head low in a rather unusual prudent fashion, but anyway I recognize him as a friend of long standing, and I am sure that he must be wrestling with this particular problem.
What happens, Mr. Speaker, is that if you live in this country anywhere outside of Vancouver, outside of Toronto or outside of Montreal, under this policy of concentration of power, deregulation and privatization of our transportation services, dismantling of our rural postal routes, you are going to be out of luck because the Tory Government has abandoned 120 years of nation building where every Canadian was to be given equal service and treated equally .They have now embraced the philosophy of the unfettered free market.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this country was not built solely on market forces. We built this country east and west and north with a railway and a national airline and a national highway and a pipeline and a broadcasting system. We built it with a public infrastructure. We built it against the pull of north/south market forces. We built a public infrastructure to bind this country together. We opposed the trade deal so vigorously because that deal was a sell-out of everything that we had stood for and upon which the country had been built. The same philosophy of the trade deal permeates the Throne Speech: laissez-faire, free market forces, neo-conservatism, profits before people, let the weak take care of themselves, the strong will profit and everything is fine, Jack.
We will be an aggressive opposition, Mr. Speaker. We are going to stand up for the less powerful in our country. We are going to continue to hold this Government to account every step of the way. We are going to monitor this trade deal. We are going to challenge the growing concentration of economic power. We are going to oppose the shut down of rural and small town Canada. We are going to highlight the despoiling of our environment. We are going to resist the deterioration of our health care and other social services. I warn the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that we are going to give the upcoming Budget sharp scrutiny.
The Prime Minister now talks about reducing the public debt. What happened since 1984? Who is responsible for the situation that this country finds itself in?
Since the Government assumed power in September, 1984, it has pushed up the public debt from $170 billion to over $320 billion today. It has piled up as much public debt as every previous Government since Confederation. It did that in only four years-despite the biggest tax increases for individuals in Canadian history. The tax increases over the last four years have been larger than they were during two world wars.
Despite the strength in the economy the Government has spent the last four years mismanaging the country's finances and piling debt on top of debt. It is now asking Canadians to pick up the tab. The Prime Minister knew the numbers. The Minister of Finance knew the numbers. They have misled Canadians. They are now going to answer to Canadians for what they have done.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

M. Turner (Vancouver Quadra)-Mr. Speaker, we must be extremely vigilant. The Government's drift, its inability to act in a coherent, thoughtful way in dealing with the great problems of this country are a serious threat to all Canadians.
This House has not sat for six months, except for a few days in December. In the meantime, a significant number of events have occurred and they have very tangibly altered the mood and the unity of our country.
Absent, invisible and silent since last fall, the Prime Minister has let the situation deteriorate to a point where basic values are now either being threatened or downright trampled underfoot.
The whole history of Canada, since the very day it was founded, reflects the fragile balance between the two founding peoples and the two language communities. It is the duty of all of us here in the House, the elected representatives of the Canadian people, to work zealously, carefully and generously to cement the links between these two language communities.
Mr. Speaker, when I entered this House for the first time in 1962, as a Member from Quebec, we were just beginning to provide services in both official languages. That was thanks to John George Diefenbaker. He must be given credit. During Mr. Pearson's administration, there was sensitivity to the problems of national unity and of accessibility for both languages, especially at the federal level to begin with. Mr. Pearson appointed Andre Laurendeau and Davie Dunton to prepare the Laurendeau-Dunton report on bilingualism and bicul-turalism.
Thanks to these inquiries, we were finally able, under Mr. Trudeau's administration, to present an official languages bill.
April 5, 1989

Then, in 1969, I was Justice Minister. I crossed the country because I had much responsibility for this bill.
I consulted the provincial governments, I negotiated with the attorneys general of the four western provinces because there were objections, I appeared before provincial legislative committees throughout Canada and, as in all cases involving language, this law to legitimize equal status for our country's two official languages was hard to accept in some parts of our country. We needed great patience and determination to reach our goal.
But we did reach it, thanks to Canadians' tolerance, generosity and good will.
I have thus spent much of my public life advancing the cause of French in Canada and especially ensuring the key position of Quebec in our Canadian Confederation.
It was in this spirit, Mr. Speaker, that in an interview with the Montreal daily Le Devoir in June 1986, I presented a reform plan to bring Quebec back to the constitutional negotiating table.
Of course Quebec is legally tied to the 1982 agreement, but the Government of Quebec did not sign the document. I do not intend to delve into the reasons for that. We had to complete the 1982 initiative so that Quebec would politically, emotionally and psychologically regain its place in the great Canadian family. We had to anchor Quebec in Canada. We had to make sure that all Quebecers, Anglophones and Francophones alike, would feel at home within the Canadian confederation.
Our non-partisan propositions did reach that objective, so much so that Premier Bourassa at the time described them as being positive, precise and concise. Despite its flaws, the agreement signed at Meech Lake a year later was indeed a step ahead. We supported it then and we still do now. However right from the beginning we kept saying here in the House and through our Senate colleagues that it had to be improved and we introduced the appropriate amendments. I am still firmly convinced that these improvements are an essential aspect of the proper balance in Canada's federalism.
Unfortunately the Prime Minister chose to take an uncompromising and radical attitude. He has systematically refused to consider our coherent and legitimate propositions. And so did the Premier of Quebec. What is worse still is that by rejecting the Supreme Court ruling on Bill 101 last December, the Premier of Quebec struck a hard blow against the spirit of national reconciliation.
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
It seems clear to me that by endorsing the concept of a distinct society in Quebec we as Members acknowledge, in the regulations and facts alike, the role and status of Quebec's Francophone majority. In the same breath, and just as clearly and as explicitely, we acknowledge the role and status of the Anglophone minority in that province. It is the fact that these two communities are jointly and solidly bound which makes Quebec distinct. My interpretation of a distinct society has been re-affirmed by the Supreme Court ruling. The Supreme Court confirmed that approach. In an enlightened and concisely drafted ruling the Court expressed the view that the language of each of the two Quebec communities ought to be reflected in the linguistic fabric of the province.
Quebec must protect, Quebec must promote the French language. Yes, that principle is absolutely essential. French must be mandatory and have priority and supremacy everywhere. There can be no exception. French must be the language of work in Quebec, at the office, in the plant and in the boardroom as well.
That is the most convincing and effective instrument to make everybody and particularly new immigrants learn French and then blend easily with Quebec's Francophone majority. The Government of Quebec has laws and regulations to preserve Quebec's identity and promote the French language. That too has been confirmed by the Supreme Court.
The federal Government has tangible means to promote French throughout the country. I would therefore urge both governments, the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier of Quebec, to take every means available to them to make French the language which all Quebecers will spontaneously use in their day to day activities. Still, it seems just as clear to me that, in Quebec as elsewhere, respect must be shown for the minorities' freedom of expression.
Well, by using the notwithstanding clause to deny the rights of Anglophone Quebecers, Mr. Bourassa not only violated the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but also his own Quebec Charter of Rights. Mr. Bourassa himself admitted it during a press conference held on March 14 when he stated, and I quote: "It is the first time in history of this province that a Quebec Premier did not hesitate to deny individual freedoms to protect and defend the French language.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
Mr. Bourassa's decision to allow Quebec's anglophone minority to use its language on indoor signs only, not even everywhere, is a superficial response to a complex question. It is a response not contemplated or permitted within the parameters of the Supreme Court judgment. It is a response which is neither good for Quebec nor good for Canada.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Every Member of the House from all sides will know that I said the same thing in the same terms when the Premier of Saskatchewan and the Premier of Alberta in turn refused to recognize the full impact of Supreme Court of Canada decisions. I said it was bad for Canada then. It is bad for Canada now. They have the same duty to protect French minority linguistic rights in their provinces that the Province of Quebec has reciprocally in Quebec.
By his silence and his inaction, the Prime Minister of Canada is an accomplice to a direct attack on the basic fundamental rights of the Quebec anglophone minority. In December I pressed him to come out strongly. You can recall the whole week of the second week of the trade debate, day after day in Question Period this Party pressed the Prime Minister for a firm position on Quebec's reaction to the Supreme Court decision and Bill 178. Because he gave us no reaction, contrast it with what he wrote a few months earlier to Premier Devine of Saskatchewan when the Supreme Court handed down its decision on the Saskatchewan language rights case. I quote the Prime Minister's letter to Premier Devine:
In its judgment, the Court observed that language rights are rooted in a deeply sensitive Canadian reality and are reflected in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which establishes among our fundamental constitutional values the acknowledgement of English and French as the official languages of this country. Thus I know you will share my view that the issues raised in the Supreme Court decision go well beyond the borders of Saskatchewan. They have implications for all provinces. Indeed, they go to the essence of the Canadian Federation.
That same letter should have been sent to Premier Bourassa in the same terms.
What did the Prime Minister say about Quebec Law 178? Nothing. What did he do about the Quebec law? Nothing. I know that I have heard in certain quarters people ask: "What are you worried about? It is just commercial signs". The Supreme Court of Canada was quite clear. Commercial signs form part of the fundamental right of free expression, and liberty of expression is part of the most essential character of liberty in this country. There is no way that any Government can duck that implication by saying it is just a matter of commercial signs.
Rights are rights, as Clifford Lincoln said in the VAssemblee Nationale the day he resigned from the Quebec Cabinet. I do not know whether there has ever been in any forum in this country in recent years a better speech than that. This is what he said:
Rights are rights. There is no such thing as inside rights and outside rights. No such a thing as rights for the tall and rights for the short. No such a thing as rights for the front and rights for the back, or rights for the east and rights for the west. Rights are links in a chain of fundamental value that binds all individuals in a society that must, to be credible, be just and fair.

Well, by using the notwithstanding clause to curtail the rights of the minority, Mr. Bourassa sent out a terrible message of intolerance. How did the Prime Minister of Canada respond, the Prime Minister whose mandate is to protect, promote, develop and saveguard our national unity? He decided to pit regions against regions. He said something in one place while his ministers said something entirely different elsewhere. Moreover, he made all sorts of statements while disregarding the true facts. He simply continued what he had done during the election campaign, Mr. Speaker. For days and weeks on end, the Conservative Leader proclaimed everywhere in Quebec that I was going to tear up the Meech Lake Accord. Well, everyone knew, including the Prime Minister, that I have always supported this Accord against hell and high water from the very beginning. In spite of the enormous difficulties I faced as a political leader because of this position, I never changed my mind, whatever the price I had to pay. Through his despicable behaviour, the Prime Minister was guilty of the worst kind of petty politics which has no place in such an important debate for the unity and future of our country.
Here is another example of his treachery. When the Supreme Court of Canada handed down its decision on Bill 101, the Prime Minister of Canada stated, and I quote:
The notwithstanding clause is inconsistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That is clear. Meanwhile, the Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Bouchard), the then Secretary of State, contended that the use of the notwithstanding clause was, in his own words, "absolutely essential".
April 5, 1989

Well, the main responsibility of the Secretary of State of Canada is to protect minorities wherever they are in this country. What an outrage! A Secretary of State directly associated with the violation of rights of both our minorities!
Again, the Prime Minister kept quiet. Not a word, not a rebuttal. Later, when we wanted to question the Secretary of State himself, he did not even show up in the House. He simply behaved in a weak and cowardly manner, preferring to hide not to have to account for his action. He tried to use the same strategy for a while yesterday. Finally, I told one of his colleagues: Canada does not operate under a presidential system but a parliamentary system. The Ministers are not here simply to make statements but also to listen. That is important.
That our Prime Minister should have done nothing is all together unacceptable. He should have corrected this situation as soon as possible. Even today, we still do not know the real position of the Government on this issue in spite of the ambiguous rhetoric used in the Speech from the Throne. The fact is, the Prime Minister has absolutely no intention of enforcing the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. So far, he has had all the time in the world and every opportunity to delete the notwithstanding clause from the Constitution. That is a proposition we had made ourselves and which was endorsed at our November 1986 Convention, but the Prime Minister would not even lift a finger. He never raised this issue with his counterparts during the Meech Lake negociations. Mr. Bourassa's offensive on the language issue, concealed with the silent support of the Prime Minister of Canada, triggered a strong reaction throughout the country.
With every passing day, those of us who have supported and still support the concept of Meech Lake meet with growing hostility towards the Accord. And this attitude contrasts with the very nature of this country and its citizens, since Canadians are first and foremost a tolerant people with an inborn sense of justice and equity. This also applies to Quebec Anglophones, whom I have had the privilege and honour of representing for many years in this House.
But, Mr. Speaker, the Anglophones from Quebec also want to protect and to promote the French language and culture. They have chosen to stay in Quebec. They are willing to work and live in French. They want to contribute to the development of the province of Quebec.
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
There is no need to suppress all the other languages to ensure the influential development of the French language. The vast majority of Quebecers, Francophones as well as Anglophones, show goodwill and an immense potential and a profound desire for cooperation.
Consequently, these feelings must be developed, this goodwill must be built upon.
While this House was not sitting, I had the opportunity to travel across Canada to over half the provinces. I found the mood of the country sour. The Meech Lake Accord is fragile. Quebec's language legislation has revived old feelings of mistrust. The repercussions of the trade deal are starting to be felt in the loss of sovereignty, the unprecedented spate of mergers and takeovers and the growth of economic concentration of power. The Government's high interest rate policy is causing hesitation and hardship. The Minister of Finance has vowed to break election promises. The Government is not enjoying a honeymoon. This Government has already dissipated the good will of Canadians.
We are a tolerant and hard working people. Generally speaking, we are receptive to the needs of others. We are willing to make sacrifices, but for us Canadians, one word is key to our response, and it is "fairness". The solution has to be fair and it has to be seen to be fair.

speechtext:
This Government has pitted region against region, favouring the wealthy and large corporate interests, leaving lower and middle class income Canadians to their own resources. This Government has demonstrated a meanness of spirit, a callous disregard for so many Canadians.
The sole value that this Government has promoted since 1984 has been money and profits and the glory of the free market. The Conservative Party and the Prime Minister see Canada as little more than a mini version of the United States. They ignore the historical, geographical and cultural differences which make us unique.
The Americans were bom of revolution. We were created by the joining of the British and French traditions. Their constitution calls for life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Ours calls for peace, order and good Government.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Right. Hon. John Turner
The American frontier has been closed for almost a century. Ours remains open. Our northern frontier is a vital symbol for us. The Americans are a giant melting pot. We are a cultural mosaic. They are unilingual. We enjoy two official languages. Ours is a parliamentary tradition. Theirs is a presidential system with the separation of powers.
We as Canadians are more influenced than any other nation on earth except perhaps the Russians by our geography, by our environment, by our vast expanse of wilderness. Americans put their faith in market forces. We put our faith in the goal of fairness and sharing, and we believe that those goals are better met with a mixed economy.
I believe that over the coming years, as Canadians, we will need to look to ourselves and to our own traditions to respond to the challenges we are going to face. This Government has not made it easier for us, because while we admire our American friends, we do not want to become American. With respect, American answers are not necessarily Canadian answers.
People from across Canada tell me that no matter how they voted, somehow they rediscovered a sense of Canadianism in themselves, that in the election, they had a very difficult decision to make: Was this good for us as a country, was this good for us as Canadians.
I believe that as Canadians, we can and will rediscover the sense of our own identity which defines us as a nation. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we in this Party intend to speak out loudly and often in this Parliament to encourage and promote that rediscovery of our identity.

Our agenda for the future includes the close monitoring of the trade deal, especially on the subsidy negotiations, to protect what is left of our sovereignty. Our agenda includes a strategic plan for our economy, a plan which incorporates the need for training and retraining for young people and for those older workers who have been displaced by new technology, a plan which has a national apprenticeship program as a central feature and reflects our firm commitment to education as a key to individual growth, to economic prosperity and to our ability to compete, a plan which recognizes and encourages the research and the development which are critical to our growth and expansion, a plan which will encourage our industries to
widen their range of trade into horizons beyond this continent into the Pacific Rim, Europe and the Third World.
Our agenda will also reflect our environmental consciousness as Canadians. A concept of sustainable development must indeed guide our economic and political decision making not only here in Canada but around the world. Our very lives and health depend on it.
The march toward real social justice must not only continue, it must be accelerated. We must forge a new social consensus which will reverse the trend under this Government of increasing the gap between rich and poor, and the fact that the fastest growing group of poor is children is a sad commentary on our failure to come to grips with the reality of poverty in our country.
We must reach our goal of full equality between men and women in all areas of our society starting with the workplace. We must once and for all recognize the legitimate aspirations, the historic aspirations, the inherent rights of the native peoples of this country and move toward self-government.
Every Canadian in eveiy part of Canada must be given an equal chance to participate fully in our country. We must convince even the most sceptical that social justice is not only fair, it is good business. The rights of the individual, for a Liberal, must remain paramount.
We must also, all of us, do our best to rekindle the bonds between our two linguistic communities, to encourage and revive the spirit of harmony and tolerance which is lacking today.
As Canadians, we must do our part to encourage the continued improvement of relations between the superpowers. The recent initiatives on disarmament are very encouraging. There are still, however, numerous regional conflicts, regional problems, around the world claiming, thousands of innocent lives, and Canadians must reclaim our leadership role in the search for peace.
I am confident that the values on which this country was built can survive. It will take great effort, more effort, to realize our vision for our country in view of the unprecedented challenges I have recited. We in this Party are committed to meeting those challenges. We will continue to fight for a more generous, fair and sovereign Canada. It is for this reason that I move, seconded by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), that the following words be added to the Address:
April 5, 1989

That this House regrets that Your Excellency's advisors continue to show indifference toward the economic and social well-being of lower and middle-income Canadians and contempt for Canadian democratic institutions by dishonouring commitments to the Canadian people with regard to the implementation of the Canada-U.S. trade deal, by abandoning Canadian farm, fisheries and forest workers, by ignoring the dangerous acceleration of concentration of corporate power, by refusing to act properly and firmly to assure public ccess to and the safety of the Canadian transportation system, by abdicating responsibility for health care, housing and senior citizens, by failing to protect the rights of minorities across Canada, by deserting the federal role in research, technological and economic development, and by circumventing the authority of the House of Commons with regard to the expenditure of public moneys and by presenting Parliament a program empty of anything save a clear desire to dismantle the Canadian social safety net while imposing an oppressive and inequitable fiscal regime.

speechtext: I find the amendment to be in order.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my view-and I suspect I am by no means unique in this regard-a Speech from the Throne ought to be a call to action to all Canadians to come together and move toward overcoming, if not actually succeeding immediately, our common problems in an equitable fashion. It should be a challenge to a nation to achieve more fairness, a greater sense of justice. It should be clear and balanced in its economics and noble in its goals.
Instead of doing this, the Government has given us a Throne Speech aimed at benefiting only one part of the Canadian community to the detriment of Canadians in all the rest of the country.
I say-and I want to make this clear in my speech as I continue this afternoon-that the Government may well have had, as it did, the organized and financial support of the business community in the election that took place last fall. But it is the people in this country who actually did the voting-including those who voted for the Conservative Party-such as nurses, fishermen, miners, loggers, steel workers, bank clerks, and housewives.
The Government we now have that has produced this Throne Speech was elected therefore by all the people. A government elected by all the people must serve the interests of all the people and not just the minority of the privileged and the powerful.
The Address-Mr. Broadbent

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Just as after the 1984 election, so too this time the Government is producing a hidden agenda. After 1984 we got the trade deal. As all Canadians know, the trade deal was not discussed at all in the 1984 campaign. And during the 1988 election we had promises not only by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulro-ney) but by candidates who are now elected as Members of Parliament for the Conservative Party, promises on economic growth, on regional development and on tax fairness.
Now we are getting a policy of slashing, cut-backs and tax increases affecting ordinary Canadians in every part of our land. Instead of inspiring Canadians with a commanding call to work for justice, this Throne Speech will do just the opposite. It will remind Canadians of what the Conservative pollsters told them before the last election, something which they have always suspected about the Conservatives: Theirs is a Party where policies and programs are not aimed at benefiting the majority. The Conservative Government is one that carries out all its objectives in the interests of all those who already have too much power and influence in our society.
I can tell you now-and the House has already seen it in the past 24 hours-that New Democratic Party Members of Parliament elected in the fall of 1988-having in particular seen this Throne Speech and having heard in the past weeks what is the real agenda of the Conservative Party-have no intention of sitting back and letting it happen. We are going to oppose with determined vigour every Bill that flows out of this Throne Speech and every budget item that will come in the weeks ahead.
Not only have the Conservatives turned up side down what they campaigned on in so many regions of the country in the fall of 1988. They have ignored one of their most crucial commitments which some of us thought at least they might take some steps toward resolving. During the election campaign and after, in the debates that took place here in the House of Commons during the Christmas period, the Government promised-in terms of the few negative consequences, which it acknowledged might flow from the great trade deal in terms of certain sectors of the economy-that it would produce a compensatory program to deal with the men and women who will be laid off in certain sectors and that it would deal with the communities so affected.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
The Prime Minister, as is his wont, characterizes the approach of the Government in terms of such words as "generous" and "massive". "Massive adjustment program" and "a generous program" were also used. Then, with typical understatement, the Prime Minister said that it would be "the finest program" that exists anywhere in the world in terms of aiding the men and women who would have inflicted upon them, as a consequence of a deal against which most Canadians voted, an economic program that forced them out of a job. We now know that the Government has no intention of doing that.
[ Translation ]
Instead of keeping its promises, the Government is examining the totally inadequate recommendations made by the Grandpre Commission. Before and during the election, business lobbyists launched an aggressive campaign to promote free trade with the Americans and support the Conservative Party. The interests of Canadian workers have been ignored so that the Government can meet the agenda set by his friends in the business world.

Since the election we have seen coming into being what clearly members of the business community had in mind when they gave support to the Conservatives in that election, and specifically for the trade deal.
In the period leading up to the Throne Speech, from speeches, from selected press releases of Ministers of the Crown, and from public comments and statements made by representatives of the business community all across the land, we have seen that the Conservatives and the business community together have one narrowly focused agenda. What they have done is to focus solely on substantial cuts to government spending and on their joint desire to impose a massive regressive new sales tax on the people of Canada. They are not going to get away with either one.

I wish to spend a minute to show that this is not simply rhetoric or a predetermined attitude that we have as a social democratic party that these results would inevitably have occurred. Sometimes we are surprised. It would have been nice to have been surprised and not to have seen the co-ordinated attack
on the people of Canada-because that is the way I wish to put it-by the business lobby and the Conservative Government in recent weeks.
The Business Council on National Issues, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the C.D. Howe Institute, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. All have had one message in their submissions to the Government in recent weeks, and in their calculated release of this information to the public of Canada in the period leading up to the Throne Speech. The message was clear: There had to be cut-backs in the public sector in general and on social programs in particular.
Members of the business community would like to convince the people of Canada that their agenda is somewhat different from that. They would like us to believe that what they are really concerned about, and exclusively concerned about, is the deficit. I do not believe for a minute that this is the case. I believe that some of them do have a concern with the deficit, and that is their priority. It is not ours.
However, there should be no illusion in our type of society-whether it is here in Canada, in western Europe, or in the United States of America-that there is an ongoing battle of power in society between those who already have substantial amounts in our economic system and the rest of the general population. That battle was being openly waged prior to the Throne Speech, and the business community saw, as a perfect instrument for gaining power, maintaining it, and using it to advantage, the Conservative Party of Canada.
If members of the business community were allegedly only concerned about the deficit, why did they not make some different proposals from the ones that they did? Why is it that they only focused on social programs and the need, to use their terms, for a "reformed" sales tax? Sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation in any society. Did members of those business groups that I have listed come forward and say: "Let us put an end to all those economically ineffective but lucrative programs that benefit us?"

That would have saved some drain on the deficit. However, they did not do that. Did they come forward and propose a minimum tax on all corporations that are profitable? This tax already exists not only in the United States of America, but also in many other industrial countries in the world? Did they do that?
April 5, 1989

The absence of such a minimum tax in Canada is also a drain on the deficit. If they were really concerned about the deficit, why did they not propose such a tax?
As my colleague, has just said, did the business community come forward and say: "My goodness, there are over $30 billion in deferred taxes out there? This is shocking. What a drain on the deficit that is. This must be stopped." Collecting such taxes would help bring down the deficit that the business community is allegedly concerned about. But no, Mr. Speaker, they did not say a word about the deferred taxes.
That is the priority of members of the business community. They are not the politicians, and that is their right in a free society. However, we should not have any illusions about what they are up to, and the net affects of such a policy. The people I hold responsible are not the private citizens in the business community. I hold responsible the Conservative politicians who form the Government of Canada.

The business community and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) have not talked about these drains on the deficit, or about these overwhelmingly ineffective economic devices that are remarkably advantageous to a certain group and, from the point of view of equity, should be radically reformed. The Minister of Finance and the business community did not talk about these at all. All they talked about was the need to have cut-backs in social programs, such as the unemployment insurance scheme or such as putting an end to universality of family allowances and cutting regional programs that are absolutely essential to average and poor families in Canada.
I remind the Conservatives who were elected that it is the average families and poor families who make up the majority of Canadians, and just once the Government should listen to a majority instead of a minority.

I heard that wonderful voice of the Minister of Finance talking from Washington, which is singularly appropriate. Michael has a tough time deciding whether he is in Ottawa or Washington. It does not
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
make a lot of difference to him. What he was saying surprised me. One of the things about the Minister of Finance, and I will be frank, is that he is normally straightforward. If he had written the Throne Speech, at least we would have got the goods straight instead of all this malarkey. We will get it straight-even if we do not like it-when we see the Budget in a few weeks.
The Minister of Finance stated that he could accept a levelling off, a turning down of the economy at this time. That is alarming, Mr. Speaker, because his argument was that the economy is overheated and as Minister of Finance he would not be unhappy to see some cooling off. We in the New Democratic Party say just the opposite at this time. Whatever Michael Wilson may think, most parts of this country have not fully recovered from the recession that began in the early 1980s. We do not say that it is time to turn down the economy. We still need economic growth in this country.

speechtext: At a time when we have more than a million men and women unemployed, it is totally irresponsible for a Minister of Finance to say he can willingly accept a downturn in the economy. We need an economic policy of growth that puts its emphasis on regional development and a tax fairness phased in over the next few years whose ultimate goal is not virtual full employment in only one part of Canada but virtual full employment from coast to coast.

We believe, as has been achieved elsewhere in this world by social democratic Governments, that we can have an approach to the economy which does not accept that we must have a trade off between unemployment and inflation. We believe that if we have the right mix of policies, of taxes and interest rates, of getting the private sector and the public sector to work together, we could achieve the goals I have just alluded to.

The growing inequity in our taxation system is flagrant. Because we have no minimum income tax for profitable corporations, the Treasury loses nearly $1 billion a year. Because large profitable corporations do not pay their fair share of income tax, Canadian families are paying more than their share.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
Instead of eliminating this inequity, the Conservatives expect to squeeze billions more out of Canadian families by introducing their new regressive sales tax. Year after year, the Auditor General points out that corporations owe billions of dollars in differed income tax. The total amount is now over $30 billion, most of which will never be paid.
The speech from the Throne contains no indication that the next Budget will oblige large corporations to pay their share.
Mr. Speaker, there are countries where corporations do pay their share, and it is high time corporations here in Canada did as well.
Mr. Speaker, to promote economic growth, it is generally desirable to promote competition. The Conservatives often talk about the importance of being competitive. However, Canada has the highest rate of corporate concentration among industrialized countries. Our economy is becoming increasingly concentrated. Nine families own 46 per cent of the total share-value of the 300 most important companies quoted on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Recently, Canadian consumers and Canadian workers who were directly affected could do nothing about the purchase of Wardair by Canadian, the Molson and Carling merger, Imperial Oil's purchase of Texaco Canada and the takeover of Consolidated Bathurst by a Chicago company. Because of the investment interest deduction, these recent mergers will cost the Treasury millions of dollars.
Instead of making decisions to remedy this situation, the minister responsible gave his blessing. Instead of changing the tax system that encourages this process, the Conservatives want to cut the budget for social programs.

What about interest rates? Interest rates stand today in the neighbourhood of 13 per cent. As our critic for financial matters pointed out in the House yesterday, real interest rates are already as high as they were at the highest peak during the Liberal's period in office at the beginning of the 1980s. At that time, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the present Minister of Finance when they were in opposition said that this was an horrendous and unacceptable situation. It was unacceptable then with a Liberal Government, and it is unacceptable now with a Conservative Government.

Such interest rates are terrible for small businesses, bad for men and women and families who want to buy homes or renew mortgages, terrible for farmers across Canada, particularly those on the Prairies where in the last few years almost nothing has gone in the right direction. Now these groups are being hit with record levels of interest rates once again.
A Government preoccupied with the issue of the deficit is well aware that for each percentage point rise in the interest rate, debt charges to the people of Canada increase by $1.5 billion. The difference in the actual interest rate and the rate projected by the Government in its 1988 Budget, if sustained for one year alone, will add a whopping $7.9 billion to the deficit for which the people of Canada will have to pay.
The Minister of Finance was in Washington at a meeting of the G-7. I do not want to pretend that the Canadian Government or any other Government could act in complete isolation from what is going on in the industrial world in terms of interest rate policy. But there is some room for freedom, and we have not exercised that. In terms of our historical relationship between Canada and the United States, we could still have lower interest rates than we now have.
There are so many Conservative Governments now in the industrial world that when the G-7 gets together it is like a meeting of the Albany Club; It is the Conservatives gathered together on a world-wide basis, regrettably with only one or two exceptions. The Government ought to be concerned about the negative effects of high interest rates in the regions outside southern Ontario and southern Quebec.
At the G-7 level, instead of automatically assuming a very conservative ideology on interest rates, there should be a determined effort by Ministers of Finance for all the industrial countries to understand what happened in the early 1980s. At that time, the same industrial countries began to increase interest rates to head off inflation. If we do that long enough, if we put millions of workers out of work, which is exactly what happened in Western Europe and North America, instead of healing a sick economy we kill a patient. This process did curtail inflation, but at untold and unacceptable costs in the life experience of millions of people here in Canada and abroad.

What our Minister of Finance ought to be doing at the G-7 meeting is trying to get the other countries there to understand the lessons from the early 1980s and to make sure that the same errors are not repeated with this lock-step high interest rate policy going into the 1990s.

speechtext: Hear, hear!
