speechtext:
Because of the cultural differences between the United States of America and Canada where profoundly different historical patterns have developed, we have said that the trade deal definition of what would constitute a subsidy inevitably would impact negatively on our capacity to have our kind of regional development policy. This was pooh-poohed by the Prime Minister before the election and during the election. It was pooh-poohed by principal spokespersons for the business community when I raised it during the course of the election. We were told not to worry about it.
We have seen the consequence already, after the deal was signed, after we got things in place in this country, after the Conservative Government did the bidding of U.S. interests. What did we see? In Cape Breton we saw the Sydney Steel Corporation being singled out by the United States. Why? It was because it receives government assistance. For the American tradition this is an unacceptable subsidy.
We have seen the same attitudes being expressed in terms of processing our fish in this country for export. For God's sake, what kind of freedom does one have as a nation-which wants to develop its own resources-if it does not retain the right to finish to whatever level of processing a product in its own country before it is

April 5, 1989
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
exported? Under this deal now the Americans are taking actions that could completely undermine the tradition that we want to add to in this Party, a tradition of practical and serious regional development policies which do indeed involve government participation with the private sector.
I want to say about this particular aspect of the trade deal that discussions are going on now between Canada and the United States on what constitutes a subsidy, or an appropriate subsidy. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that all the members of the New Democratic Party caucus, no matter from where they come, have an interest in Canada as a whole. We are going to do everything we can to assure that at least the traditional Canadian definition of what constitutes an appropriate and acceptable definition of regional development policy will remain in Canada.
On the same issue of regional fairness in this country, some of us were not entirely surprised when in the past 10 days we heard that the Government froze the discussions that were going on with the provinces concerning regional development policy. Suddenly, they all came to a halt. We know why. What the Government is going to do is put a freeze on funds that were traditionally going out in recent years in adequate amounts to the provinces for regional development. We will see the final results of this, of course, when we see the Budget of the Minister of Finance.
The Government's adherence to the simplistic and self-serving big business agenda is also seen very clearly in its response to the problems of VIA Rail. VIA Rail, the passenger aspect of rail transportation in our country, has its equivalents in every successful industrial country in western Europe. It has its equivalent now in the United States, where even the United States has put public capital into Amtrak to make sure it works.
A few years ago the Conservatives blasted the Liberals at the time-and I was amused to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) say today that the Conservatives are going to be doing some wicked things about VIA Rail. I was here in 1980, and I say to the Leader of the Opposition that it was the Liberals who cut VIA Rail first, not the Conservatives. The present Leader of the Opposition is saying that he was not here.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is right. You were making a good speech.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say to the Leader of the Opposition that if he was not here then, he may not be here in a short period of time either, and the Liberal Party is the Liberal Party. It said one thing when it was in power and another thing after.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I want to say not only to the Leader of the Opposition, who agrees right now with the position that we are taking on VIA Rail, but to others that this is important. It is important in most regions of Canada including where there are many Conservative seats. I am sure they are following with interest the debate on VIA Rail. It is an essential public service that can be made profitable.
I have had occasion, with my caucus colleagues, to meet representatives of Atlantic Canada today about VIA Rail. I pointed out to them that in my constituency of Oshawa, in the automotive sector for passenger travel, the company called General Motors put $2 billion of investment into one little community. General Motors does not expect to have a return within weeks or within months on that investment. General Motors plans years down the road to get a return on that investment. We say that there is only one group in our society that will make sure that VIA Rail will pay off in the future, and that is the people of Canada. Only the people of Canada through the Government of Canada can put money into VIA Rail to make it exciting and a much better service. It is good now, but the service could be much better, and the people of Canada through the Government of Canada should be doing that.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I say to some of the Conservatives here today who may have a bit of interest in this issue that one of the new bits of information I got from listening to people today was to learn Bombardier, a Canadian company, is currently supplying new equipment to Amtrak in the United States. It is not only supplying equipment to make Amtrak better, but it is doing so with subsidies from the Canadian Government through the Export Development Corporation.
April 5, 1989

Canadian taxpayers are helping Bombardier sell equipment to make Amtrak better for American passengers. I say to the Conservative Government: "If you can subsidize rail service in the United States, why can't you do it even more effectively here in Canada?"

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As I said, Mr. Speaker, in a different context instead of derailing VIA Rail, why does the Government not simply sink its nuclear submarine policy?

speechtext: Hear, hear!

There are a couple of other priorities that we in this Party believe that this Government should be addressing in a much more serious way which have either been inadequately dealt with or ignored. One of these I want to mention is child care. The policy announced by the Government prior to the last election concerned every person working in the field-man, woman, easterner, westerner, Quebecois.

Quebecers or citizens of another region.

Everyone who knew something about child care condemned the program. There was not an expert that I talked to who thought it was effective. It seemed merely to be a politically expedient scheme so the Conservatives could say they were going to do something about child care. It was very regressive, as we pointed out at the time. It was to provide less money for new child care spaces than was already in the works under existing programs.
I had hoped that at least in this area of social policy the Government of Canada would have been responding to the real needs of our people and would have come back and said: "We are going to bring in child care. We are going to produce a child care program that is going to be universally accessible, that is going to be adequate for our children, and that is going to be available at a reasonable cost, at a rate that all people who need it can afford". That is what they should have been doing.
I want to say, in particular as a man, that it is important for future families that child care be available and that it meet the real needs of our children, as they are the ones who are affected by this. The family structure is so profoundly changed from the days when I grew up. At
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
some point one hopes men and women will share the parental burden on an equal basis, but we are kidding ourselves if we do not understand the real problem today. In terms of psychological requirement if I can put it that way, women want to work. Most of them are now outside the home. For culturally induced reasons they have feelings, much more profound than those of us of the male sex, in that they need to look after children.
We should understand that, if we really believe that a woman ought to have a real choice not just an abstract choice to stay at home, which is a desirable and legitimate choice. If a woman really wants to get out and work and feel that her children are going to be adequately looked after, we need an adequate child care program.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you look at the Conservative Throne Speech and at all the statements that were made by the Ministers before it was presented, and what surely we are going to be getting from the Minister of Finance when he brings down his Budget, you will see that it means only one thing, that the persistent high levels of unemployment will remain and probably get worse. There will be an increase, not a reduction, in corporate concentration. There will be an exacerbation, not a reduction in regional tension. There will be cuts to social programs like unemployment insurance. There will be more money for the wealthy and less for the poor, greater benefits for large corporations and less for the smaller.
This need not be the case. It must not be the case and it would not be the case if we had a New Democratic Party Government in Canada. I can tell you that.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What we need is imaginative leadership which understands that economic policy must transcend the narrow priorities of one part of the Canadian community. With the right mix of policies, as I have said, on interest rates, on taxes, on investment in the private and public sector, with anti-inflation policies that are directed at certain regions when inflation occurs there, we can build the kind of Canada that would go way beyond the dreams of those who currently hold power in this Parliament.
I want now to say something about the environment, Mr. Speaker.

April 5, 1989
The Address-Mr. Broadbent

We have inherited one of the most beautiful countries on this planet. Travelling from Newfoundland to Vancouver, from Whitehorse to Quebec City in any season is always very pleasant. For too long we have ravaged the beauty of our country and threatened the heritage of future generations with disappearance.
As the Brundtland Commission has shown, as television reports have illustrated, as all children now know, the problem of the environment, from the forests of Brazil to the ozone layer, is global. The future of the human race depends on concerted, well-chosen international political action. All governments must commit themselves to sustainable economic development and respect for our environment. Yes, the problem is global, but to obtain concrete results, each country must act on its own territory. Otherwise, this noble objective will become another overlooked cliche!
Consider the response of the Government to the oil spill almost two weeks ago and to another one off the west coast of Vancouver Island three months ago. We have seen a Government that has learned all the right cliches.
During the last election campaign I was proud of my Party which had, months before the election, laid out serious proposals on the environment. We were proud to take that to the people of Canada in the fall of 1988. Suddenly the Government, no doubt after it did its polling, found that the people of Canada were light years ahead of it on the environment. It began to talk about the environment during the election. The new Minister has talked about the environment since. Canadians are fed up with talk. They want to see some concrete action from the Government on the question of the environment.
Nothing was so indicative of its seeming opaqueness on the subject as the Minister's reply in the House today. The people of Vancouver Island are still working on a spill that took place three months ago. First, the Minister even refused to answer the question. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) acted as if everything was fine, nothing needed to be done and the Government was not responsible for the fiasco three months ago.
We believe there should be a royal commission that could act quickly and thoroughly on this subject. There are problems now, but if we do not take corrective action there will be problems in the future and the Government will be held responsible. In that context, some of the specific proposals I want to put forward now are drafted in such a way that we put legal obligations on the Government rather than depend simply on political will.

The Parliament of Canada must take the following action during the next session.
First, pass a charter of environmental rights that would give citizens access to all environmental information and the right to sue governments on environmental matters.
Show that we are as concerned about the environment as we are about property by including in the Criminal Code penalties for serious environmental infractions.
Pass a law requiring Cabinet to make all its economic decisions comply with the principle of sustainable development.
This is absolutely necessary to give real meaning to what the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment have said about sustainable development.
Canadian legislation must be clear and override the trade agreement, which fundamentally contradicts the principle of sustainable development.
From now on, the protection of our land, our air, our water and our trees must not be negotiable. That is our policy.

I want to turn now to foreign policy. There has been what can only be described as the most serious absence of leadership by the Government on foreign policy issues. It is either doing nothing, doing it too late, or the Prime Minister is saying one thing while the Secretary of State for External Affairs is saying another.
The Government was the last representative of a country in the western world to recognize that Chairman Arafat had something positive, necessary and long overdue to say in his statements in Algiers and Geneva. The situation in the Middle East is terribly complex. I will not presume to be an expert on it, but some of us have followed it carefully and know that some of the conditions which have to be met include Palestinian rights and the right of Israel to exist. Israel is a good friend of Canada and there is no change in that policy. But it is totally unacceptable to the people of Canada for Canada
April 5, 1989

to lag so far behind in accepting change when it has taken place in that part of the world.
I said on other occasions that the Prime Minister at one point showed leadership in the Commonwealth on the South African issue. I heard from others who were at the meeting that on one important occasion the Prime Minister took on the Prime Minister of Great Britain in a commendable fashion in the interest of the black majority of South Africa. Again, the Government seems to have taken a fashionable approach to international politics as it has done with other issues.
What seems to have been the policy a few years ago has been dropped by the Government. The leadership that was forthcoming then has been abandoned because the Government has refused to follow through on the Prime Minister's 1985 commitment at the United Nations to produce a comprehensive set of sanctions against South Africa, as we ought to have in place.
Let us turn to East-West relations. Beyond any question, in terms of its ultimate impact on Canada and the world, the relationship between the Soviet Bloc and Western Bloc is by far the most important.
In saying this, I may obviously and clearly be wrong in my judgment, but if one looks at the history of the 20th century, apart from the abomination of the Second World War, two globally significant people in terms of their impact on history have emerged. One of them was Lenin, most of whose consequences I frankly suggest were negative, whatever the aspirations. When Lenin arrived at the Finland station in the early part of this century, history in a global sense began to move in one direction.
The other man of great and world significance who has come on the scene-and we must understand that he is trying to undo so much that has been wrong-is Mr. Gorbachev of the Soviet Union. We should understand that and give support to those remarkable reforms that have been taking place.
I ask all Members of the House, particularly those in the Government of Canada, to think about the changes that have been made in the last three years by this remarkable man and the obviously progressive people with him. Let us consider the unilateral action that has been taken by the Soviet Union, such as on site inspection in the Soviet Union.
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
I recall talking to Mr. Gorbachev when he was here before he became the head of his Party. The issue of on site inspection in the Soviet Union was discussed. He intimated in conversation that it may happen. It was never accepted before. There is now on site inspection in the Soviet Union.
There is the unilateral withdrawal from Afghanistan, uncensored news reports, the travels of Sakharov and Bonner. There is the permission of critical theatre and printing. There is even an open competition for election, albeit within a one-Party system, but we will watch and see what happens with that.
There have been remarkable changes in that society in the last few years, and I repeat that they were unilateral. I also say on behalf not only of my colleagues, but, I am sure, of progressive and humane people in Canada and all over the world, that they were changes that were overdue and desirable. But what remarkable tenacity and courage must have been required by a number of people in that very different society from ours who launched them. So I am saying, therefore, if these changes are going on in a country that will have a major impact on the world, whether we like it or not, Canada should not be ignoring these initiatives. We should be responding by taking initiatives of our own as a country.
Surely we must understand in the West that if Mr. Gorbachev and what he stands for fails, the situation will not get better, it will get worse, and we will see or could see the return of the Cold War and all that that could mean, first and foremost for the people of the Soviet Union themselves, but also for us in terms of international politics.
This move toward democracy in the Soviet Union is important to men and women in the Soviet Union, important to men and women in the Baltic states, important to the people of East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. It is important to men and women all over the world.
We have a role to play. It is a minor role, but it should not be dismissed. We have exercised that role in the past and surely we should be doing it now. I ask on behalf of the people of Canada, where is the Canadian voice?

April 5, 1989
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
A current discussion within NATO, for example, has Margaret Thatcher wanting to modernize nuclear weapons. Chancellor Kohl of West Germany is undecided, but the Prime Minister of Norway and the head of the Government in Spain are opposed and are openly saying that they should not be modernized. I say that instead of sitting back and watching the debate take place between Margaret Thatcher on one hand and Mrs. Brundtland on the other, the Prime Minister of Canada should make our position clear, and we should say that we are against the modernization of nuclear weapons.
There are other things that we can do to complement in part what I have said already are the unilateral actions by the Soviet Union. We can get rid of that decision to build nuclear submarines that is economically foolish and irresponsible in terms of world peace. We should say no to that right away. We should also put an end to the tests of air-launched Cruise missiles.
Again, I talked about that particular issue with Mr. Gorbachev when he was in this country, and he was quite candid in what he had to say. If we want to move in a sensible direction there, we should say we will put an end to tests in Canada. And then we could say to the Soviets, who are our northern neighbours: Let us initially have a joint treaty whereby they will not hold any tests and we will not hold any tests, and let us develop verification procedures together, because the Cruise field is complex. Let us try that, and then we could make it the basis, perhaps, of a global test. We are their northern neighbour. We have access. We have a role to play and that would be a constructive initiative. It would be something useful. I again say to the Prime Minister: "Get out and do it".
I also say that we should take seriously, instead of dismissing cynically, what Mr. Gorbachev had to say about the Arctic. We should test him on the seriousness of his proposals by talking about the Kola Peninsula and see just how seriously they are prepared to make changes in that part of the world.
In this context, I want to say that these kinds of steps taken by a Canadian leader ought not to be seen, as is so often suggested by Conservatives, as anti-American. The low level of argumentation that has to be dealt with is almost embarrassing. Anyway, look at Mr. Pearson, a Canadian Prime Minister, not of my Party, obviously. He incurred the wrath of Lyndon Johnson at one time on Vietnam. Pierre Trudeau's disarmament moves annoyed
Ronald Reagan. Mr. Diefenbaker, I remember at one time, did the same thing about Bomarc missiles.
I say to our Prime Minister that these Canadians did not do it because they were anti-American or to annoy the Americans. They did it because they were interested in making some realistic Canadian contribution to peace, and they stood up as independent Canadians and understood that the United States is a different country and that we can make our own polices.
I want to conclude my remarks in this vein by saying to the Prime Minister, certainly go to Moscow. Go without illusions, but understand that the Soviet Union has changed. Go there, speak up for freedom, speak up for disarmament, speak up for global peace. Do this and you will have every New Democrat, every Liberal, every Canadian in the country, I am sure, behind you, but go, Mr. Prime Minister, and do those things.
I want to conclude by saying that Governments, in my view, should be acting at home and abroad, in domestic and foreign policy, to promote the confidence and the security of the people of Canada. Now is the time to use the instruments of government to meet the needs of Canadians for jobs, for child care, for safe transportation, for environmental protection, and for regional fairness. Now is the time for lower interest rates, strong regional development programs and corporate tax reform. Now is the time to promote greater fairness and equality within Canada and peace and disarmament in the world at large. Now is the time to do our part, not complacently to leave Canada as it is but to see and achieve what Canada might become.
Having said that, I want to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kamloops (Mr. Riis):
That the amendment be amended by adding the following words: 'And specifically regrets the failure of the Government to protect the environment through the criminalization of environmental offences and thorough review of the environmental impact of government initiatives: to establish a national child care program with national objectives of care; to provide a coherent, well-articulated foreign policy for Canada at a time when leadership is required; to put the needs of ordinary Canadians ahead of those of its corporate friends; to make sure that wealthy Canadian corporations and individuals carry their fair share of the tax burden; to provide assistance to workers dislocated by the trade deal and/or corporate restructuring; to meet the needs of Canada's regions; or to commit itself to a policy of full employment for all Canadians; and finally to ameliorate the harm caused to Canadian families and regions through its high interest policy.
